label: Childhood
tagline: Joy is expected, scaffolded, and increasingly assessed
mainTransition: From embodied and relational joy toward school-mediated evaluation and structured accomplishment.

label: Adolescence
tagline: Joy becomes socially mediated, visible, and comparative
mainTransition: Play does not disappear; it becomes socially regulated through identity, status, surveillance, credentials, and platform visibility.

label: Adulthood
tagline: Joy must be justified, optimized, purchased, or made productive
ageRangeLabel: Approximately 25 onward, with subgroups determined less by age alone than by work, care, economic security, and health.
mainTransition: Play is often treated as a reward after work, a purchasable experience, a wellness tool, a performance of identity, or an optimization mechanism—rather than a legitimate dimension of ordinary life.

label: Infancy and early caregiving
centralJoyMode: Sensory pleasure, attachment, movement, shared attention, laughter, repetition
rewardSystemShift: Caregiver attunement and comfort are the principal regulatory system; joy is largely relational and embodied

label: Toddlerhood and early autonomy
centralJoyMode: “I do it myself,” imitation, pretend, messy experimentation, object play
rewardSystemShift: Adult approval and boundaries enter more visibly; praise can either support agency or become controlling

label: Early childhood / imaginative play
centralJoyMode: Pretend worlds, role play, absurdity, storytelling, social play, sensory making
rewardSystemShift: Preschool routines, behavioral charts, developmental milestones, and branded media begin organizing play

label: Middle childhood / school-age play
centralJoyMode: Peer play, games, collecting, making, competition, skill-building, rule negotiation
rewardSystemShift: Grades, standardized comparison, sports ranking, extracurricular credentials, screen engagement metrics become more salient

label: Early transition to adolescence
centralJoyMode: Belonging, identity experimentation, group humor, fandom, gaming, social media
rewardSystemShift: Likes, follows, appearance feedback, academic sorting, and peer comparison become increasingly intertwined

label: Early adolescence
centralJoyMode: Friendship, humor, fandom, games, music, experimenting with self-presentation
rewardSystemShift: Peer approval, school ranking, body/image norms, early social metrics

label: Middle adolescence
centralJoyMode: Skill development, subcultures, team activity, creative production, romantic connection
rewardSystemShift: Academic competition, extracurricular achievement, likes/follows, gaming rank, parental monitoring

label: Late adolescence / emerging adulthood
centralJoyMode: Independence, collective projects, nightlife, making, political/creative communities, experimentation
rewardSystemShift: College admissions, employability, internships, personal branding, debt, productivity tools

label: Early working adulthood
centralJoyMode: Building relationships, exploration, hobbies, travel, creative identity, gaming, nightlife
rewardSystemShift: Career precarity, debt, productivity apps, professional visibility, side-hustle pressure

label: Established adulthood
centralJoyMode: Family/social rituals, craft, social hobbies, community participation, home-based play
rewardSystemShift: Promotion, caregiving, household logistics, financial obligations, time scarcity

label: Later adulthood
centralJoyMode: Generativity, cultural participation, mentoring, companionship, hobbies, play with younger generations
rewardSystemShift: Retirement security, health constraints, age norms, caregiving, digital inclusion/exclusion

label: Later life / elderhood
centralJoyMode: Connection, reminiscence, embodied or adapted play, storytelling, intergenerational contact
rewardSystemShift: Care systems, accessibility, mobility, institutional routines, social isolation

label: Intrinsic joy capacity
description: The ability to pursue activity for curiosity, pleasure, meaning, exploration, play, or connection without needing an external payoff

label: Extrinsic reward orientation
description: Increased reliance on approval, grades, metrics, money, streaks, status, likes, or productivity as reasons to act

label: Joy deficit
description: A structural imbalance in which attention, time, design resources, and social legitimacy privilege rewardable productivity and screen stimulation over direct connection and open-ended play

label: Burnout / alienation
description: Exhaustion, reduced agency, cynicism, depleted curiosity, and difficulty accessing pleasure outside reward or escape loops

label: Restorative adult play
description: Voluntary, socially meaningful, materially or bodily engaging activity that restores autonomy, relatedness, curiosity, and non-instrumental enjoyment

label: Education system
leadsTo: The extent to which play is protected or subordinated to achievement

label: Platform, media, and AI system
leadsTo: The cultural expectation of instantaneous stimulation

label: Free exploration, curiosity, and willingness to make mistakes
Intrinsic competence
description: “I can try because I want to know,” rather than “I must perform to be approved.”

label: Access to loose parts, ordinary objects, outdoor space, art materials, and peer time
Choice, negotiation, experimentation, and tolerance for ambiguity
Later ability to enjoy activities without prescribed outcomes
School systems, behavioral charts, grades, and praise framed around “being smart,” speed, or compliance
Attention shifting from process to evaluation
Performance monitoring
description: “Am I doing this correctly?”

label: External reward orientation
description: Especially when mistakes carry social or institutional consequences.

label: Children’s media, retailers, licensors, influencers, and toy manufacturers
Branded character attachment and collectible desire
Learned association between play, acquisition, novelty, and identity display
Later adult collecting, fandom, blind-box consumption, and nostalgia markets
description: Can later feed these.

label: Community and creative practices
description: Can also offer these.

label: Visibility as a condition of belonging
Comparison of appearance, popularity, skill, lifestyle, and consumption
External validation-seeking
description: Through likes, rankings, streaks, follower counts, gaming levels, or social approval.

label: Admissions systems, standardized testing, college/career advice, and parental anxiety
Question shift: from “Do I enjoy this?” to “Will this help me get in, get hired, or stand out?”
Instrumentalized leisure
description: Creative activity may remain pleasurable but becomes burdened by evaluation.

label: Notifications, streaks, variable feedback, rank progression, loot systems, and infinite feeds
Engagement data produces revenue and optimization feedback for platforms
Shared fandoms, tabletop games, creative communities, modding, cosplay, music scenes, and collaborative making
Social connection and low-stakes identity exploration
Intrinsic joy
description: When participants retain autonomy and community ownership.

label: Commercialization through influencer economies and monetized visibility
description: The same spaces may be commercialized.

label: Housing costs, debt, precarious employment, health insurance systems, and wage stagnation
Perceived need for constant employability, skill acquisition, and availability
Self-optimization
description: Tracking, upskilling, side hustles, personal branding, and difficulty resting.

label: Joy deferral
description: Play must be earned, justified, monetized, or transformed into self-improvement.

label: Managers, enterprise software, performance dashboards, communication tools, and AI systems
Increased measurement and expectations of responsiveness
Higher output expectations, verification work, tool switching, and constant adaptation
description: AI can automate or assist tasks, but in many settings it also leads to these.

label: Less recovery time and reduced autonomy
Diminished curiosity and energy for self-directed play
description: Burnout diminishes curiosity and energy, producing the joy deficit.

label: Streaming services, social media, mobile games, retail platforms, and notification systems
Short-term gratification, passive consumption, or repetitive checking
description: Often chosen because exhausted people have limited time and energy.

label: Low-recovery entertainment
description: Can lead to less sleep, less direct sociality, and less capacity for effortful but restorative play.

label: LEGO, tabletop games, miniatures, craft kits, collectibles, fidget objects, hobby stores, maker communities, toy designers, and convention cultures
Adult access to playful objects and rituals
Relaxation, flow, tactile engagement, creativity, nostalgia, identity exploration, and social belonging
Scarcity-based purchasing, speculative collecting, status display, or blind-box reward loops
Community centers, libraries, parks, game cafés, workshops, unions, local clubs, friend groups, public festivals, and shared meals
Belonging, laughter, cooperation, and shared ritual
Relatedness
description: One of the core psychological needs associated with self-motivation and wellbeing (Self-Determination Theory).

label: Greater reliance on convenient, screen-based entertainment
Family rituals
description: Games, shared meals, humor, crafting, storytelling.

label: Intergenerational models of joy and relatedness
Testing, grading, ranking, attendance, behavioral management
External evaluation as the normal condition of learning
Recess, arts, drama, music, workshop learning, exploratory pedagogy
Wage conditions, debt, housing, healthcare, childcare costs
Output visibility as a proxy for value
Leisure industry and adult toy market
Metrics
description: Likes, streaks, points, rank, followers, badges, view counts.

label: Anticipation, repeat checking, and measurable engagement
Personalized consumption pathways and narrowed attention
Increased output expectations and homogenized, tool-directed creative labor
Moralization of output and guilt about rest
Adult shame around play and material delight
Can instrumentalize joy as another performance requirement
Reopens access to toys and play
The child learns to seek approval, grades, or winning.
These outcomes make adults allocate more attention and opportunities to measurable achievement.
Unstructured play appears less defensible or “less valuable.”
Reduced unstructured play further increases reliance on externally organized stimulation.
Measurable competence
description: Reinforcing loop that shifts joy from self-directed exploration toward performance.

label: Young people engage in art, sport, games, volunteering, or making.
Institutions ask them to document outcomes, awards, leadership, audience size, or market value.
Activities gain prestige when they become legible as credentials.
Time flows toward credential-bearing activity and away from private, purposeless play.
The cultural expectation that every activity should “count” becomes stronger.
Play becomes proof
description: Reinforcing institutional–cultural loop.

label: Technology or AI reduces the time needed for a task.
Employers, clients, institutions, or the individual raise the expected volume, speed, and availability of output.
Time savings are absorbed rather than converted into rest, play, or connection.
Fatigue increases, making low-effort digital rewards more attractive.
Reduced recovery lowers creative capacity and intrinsic motivation.
Lower capacity is interpreted as a personal failure to optimize, restarting the drive for productivity tools.
Productivity ratchet
description: Reinforcing socio-technical extraction loop.

label: Extrinsic-reward displacement
description: Reward conditioning → motivational displacement → reinforcing loop.

label: More perceived need to work or optimize
Time scarcity and depleted play
description: Structural pressure → depletion → convenience substitution → reinforcing loop.

label: Play-to-productivity capture
description: Institutional capture / commodification / autonomy erosion.

label: Capacity to sustain relationships and collective spaces
Social play as restoration
description: Enabling condition → social reinforcement → regenerative loop. The primary counter-loop.

label: Work-time regulation, leave, flexible work, and social support
description: Protective-policy reference (Denmark), not proof of a universally “happier culture.”
caution: Comparative example; outcomes are shaped by many interacting welfare, labor-market, and cultural conditions.

datapoints.label: Satisfaction with time use (OECD, cited cross-country data)

label: Game and character-industry ecosystem
description: Ambivalent play-economy reference (Japan): globally influential games and character industries show how adult-oriented play, collecting, fandom, and creative communities can be culturally legitimate while also deeply commercialized and platform-mediated.
connectionTypes: cultural legitimacy + commercial extraction; explicitly double-edged
caution: Explicitly double-edged: cultural legitimacy and commercial extraction coexist.

label: Protected unstructured time
effect: Interrupts early performance conditioning and adult time scarcity

label: Non-evaluative feedback
effect: Interrupts the shift from curiosity to approval-seeking

label: Open-ended playful object
effect: Reinforces autonomy, tactile exploration, ambiguity, repetition without scoring

label: Anti-extractive digital interaction
effect: Interrupts streaks, metrics, infinite feeds, and attention capture

label: Adult third place for play
effect: Reinforces relatedness and recurring, low-cost social play

label: Play without proof ritual
effect: Interrupts portfolio logic, content creation pressure, and instrumental leisure

label: Workplace recovery boundary
effect: Interrupts AI-enabled output escalation and always-on availability

label: Alternative success metric
effect: Redefines value around agency, connection, delight, and restoration rather than output alone

label: Accessible material play kit
effect: Lowers barriers of money, confidence, time, and “childishness” stigma

label: Intergenerational play format
effect: Counteracts age segregation and normalizes play across life stages
